newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany clamps down on "extremists" in cyberspace.
newsitem.headline: Germany clamps down on "extremists" in cyberspace.

text.p: Stepping up their crusade to stamp out extremism in cyberspace, German prosecutors said on Friday they had filed charges against a left-wing politician in a case that could further extend the growing reach of Internet law.
Prosecutors broke new ground in pursuing, in this case, not an extremist publication but someone accused of leading others to "suspect" Internet pages through their own home page.

Berlin prosecutors are investigating Angela Marquardt, a 25-year-old deputy leader of Germany's reform communist Party of Democratic Socialism (PDS), to see if she broke the law by putting a "hyperlink" on her home page to the Radikal magazine.
"It is illegal in Germany to teach others how to commit a felony or to sanction a felony," Berlin prosecutor's office spokesman Ruediger Reiff told Reuters.

"Those who committed the initial crime of writing the articles in Radikal are as yet unidentified, but Ms. Marquardt appears to have committed the crime of aiding this felony. Press freedom does not go that far."
Radikal has been banned from publishing an article in Germany with instructions on how to sabotage railway lines.

Although Radikal's Internet magazine is located on a computer in the Netherlands, prosecutors argue Marquardt could be charged for aiding and abetting the original crime because the hyperlink on her page allows others access to Radikal.
A hyperlink is a section of highlighted text on a page which can be viewed on the World Wide Web, the popular graphical part of the Internet computer network.
By clicking on the hyperlink with a computer mouse, the viewer is catapulted across the Internet to another computer where the linked document has been stored.

"You are charged with a wilfully initiated illegal act: disturbing the public peace by distributing texts which sanction dangerous offences against the public," prosecutors said in a letter which Marquardt published on her Web page.
This is not the first time German prosecutors have tried to stop authors of electronic publications from saying things on the Internet they would not be allowed to publish in print.
The commercial online service CompuServe was forced in 1995 to block access to some 200 Internet "news groups", because some of them were being used to spread child pornography illegal in Germany.

Toronto-based neo-Nazi Ernst Zuendel has also been the subject of the government's ire for publishing articles on the Internet that deny the fact that millions of Jews died in the Holocaust. This is also a crime in Germany.
In both of those cases, the government initially tried to press charges against the access provider, CompuServe, but later decided there were no grounds for charges.
CompuServe blocked access for its members to Marquardt's homepage in September, saying the link to Radikal violated its policies on content. Prosecutors said CompuServe was not under investigation.
Marquardt, has since changed the address of her homepage. Writing on the page, she attacked the charges as "censorship".

"The charges make direct reference to my function as deputy chairman of the PDS. This is hardly about building bombs or detailed directions to train lines and their weak spots," she wrote. "This is about creating a clean, tame public, a living room atmosphere in cyberspace."
